title: Product, service and channel management
objective: Manage a product through its life cycle, build a product mix and brand, and choose the channel that gets it to customers.
body:
Product questions ask what to sell and how to manage it over time; channel questions ask how it reaches the customer. Both appear constantly on the exam and in buying, merchandising and service role-plays.

**Product levels and the product mix.** A product is a bundle of benefits: the *core* benefit (what the customer really buys, such as transportation), the *actual* product (features, design, brand, packaging) and the *augmented* product (warranty, delivery, installation, service). A company's *product mix* is everything it sells. *Width* is the number of product lines; *depth* is the number of versions within a line. Adding a new flavor to an existing line is a *line extension*; putting an established brand name on a new category is a *brand extension*.

**Branding and packaging.** Strong brands build recognition and loyalty. *Brand equity* is the extra value a well-known name adds, which lets a firm charge more and launch new products more easily. A *manufacturer (national) brand* is owned by the producer; a *private (store) brand* is owned by the retailer. Packaging protects, promotes and informs, and labels must meet legal requirements.

**Product life cycle (PLC).**
1. *Introduction*: low sales, high costs, informative promotion to build awareness.
2. *Growth*: sales climb quickly, competitors enter, profits rise.
3. *Maturity*: sales level off and competition is fiercest; firms defend share with promotion, pricing and small improvements.
4. *Decline*: sales fall; firms cut costs, harvest remaining profit or drop the product.

**Services.** Services are *intangible* (they can't be touched before purchase), *inseparable* (produced and consumed at the same time), *perishable* (an empty seat can't be stored and sold later) and *variable* (quality depends on who delivers it and when). Marketers respond with tangible cues, staff training, scheduling and demand-based pricing.

**Channels of distribution.** A *direct channel* goes from producer to consumer; an *indirect channel* adds intermediaries such as wholesalers, retailers or agents. Intermediaries add value by breaking bulk, storing goods, financing, sharing risk and building assortments. *Distribution intensity* fits the product: *intensive* (everywhere, for convenience goods like gum), *selective* (some outlets, for shopping goods like jeans) or *exclusive* (one dealer per area, for luxury or specialty goods). Disagreements among channel members are *channel conflict*.

**Common mistake:** treating the PLC as a calendar. Products move through stages based on sales and competition, not time, and smart management can extend maturity for decades.
examples: A company with 4 product lines (shampoo, conditioner, body wash, lotion) offering 6 scents each has a product-mix width of 4 and a depth of 6 in every line.
A luxury watchmaker allows only one authorized dealer per metro area. Exclusive distribution protects its premium image and gives dealers a reason to invest in service.
A theater sells discounted rush tickets an hour before the show because an unsold seat is worth nothing once the curtain rises: service perishability.

questions.stem: Sales of a smartwatch model have leveled off, many competitors offer similar features, and the brand is spending more on promotion to defend its share. Which life-cycle stage is it in?
questions.explanation: Flat sales, crowded competition and spending to defend share are signs of maturity. In growth, sales would still be climbing quickly.

questions.stem: Customers of a hair salon get noticeably different results depending on which stylist they see. Which characteristic of services does this show?
questions.explanation: Variability means service quality depends on who provides it and when. Salons reduce it with training and standard procedures.

questions.stem: A gum manufacturer wants its product sold in grocery stores, gas stations, vending machines, pharmacies and airport kiosks. Which distribution strategy is this?
questions.explanation: Convenience goods such as gum need intensive distribution, meaning as many outlets as possible, because shoppers won't search for them.

questions.stem: A snack company has 3 product lines: chips in 8 flavors, pretzels in 4 varieties and popcorn in 6 varieties. What are the width of its product mix and the average depth of its lines?
questions.explanation: Width is the number of lines, 3. Average depth is the total number of items divided by lines: (8 + 4 + 6) ÷ 3 = 18 ÷ 3 = 6.

questions.stem: A well-known sports-drink brand launches a line of protein bars under the same brand name. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Using an established brand name in a new product category is a brand extension. A line extension would be a new flavor of the same sports drink.

questions.stem: A supermarket chain sells canned vegetables under its own store name at lower prices than the national brands beside them. These products are examples of:
questions.explanation: Private (store) brands are owned by the retailer rather than the producer. Manufacturer brands are owned by the company that makes the product.

questions.stem: A wholesaler buys 10,000 cases of paper towels from a manufacturer and resells them to small neighborhood stores in batches of 20 cases. Which marketing function is the wholesaler performing?
questions.explanation: Breaking bulk means dividing large quantities into smaller amounts that buyers can use. Assorting would combine products from several producers into one offering.

questions.stem: A clothing brand begins selling online at prices lower than its retail partners charge, and the retailers complain that they are losing sales. What is this an example of?
questions.explanation: Channel conflict is disagreement among members of a distribution channel, often caused when a producer competes with its own retailers.

questions.stem: A laptop seller includes free setup, a two-year warranty and next-day delivery with every purchase. These extras belong to which product level?
questions.explanation: The augmented product adds services and support beyond the physical item. The actual product is the laptop's features, design and brand.

questions.stem: A DVD player's sales have fallen about 30% a year for three straight years. Which action best fits this stage of the product life cycle?
choices: Spend heavily on informative ads to build awareness
Cut costs and promotion, then decide whether to harvest or discontinue it
Add many new models to win rivals' customers
Raise the price to skim early adopters
questions.explanation: Steady, steep sales declines mark the decline stage, where firms reduce costs and either harvest remaining profits or drop the product.

flashcards.definition: The number of different product lines a company sells.
The number of versions, such as sizes, flavors or models, offered within one product line.
The added value a well-known brand name gives a product, allowing higher prices and easier launches.
The stages a product moves through in the market: introduction, growth, maturity and decline.
Services can't be stored for later sale, so unused capacity such as an empty seat is lost revenue.
Selling through a limited number of chosen outlets in an area, common for shopping goods.
